value_chain_position: Motion control & automation equipment toll-taker — sells cobots, AMRs, and chip/system ATE hardware into every factory-automation and chip-test buildout
cost_curve_verified: Disagree, and the deterministic screener figures are the ones that are wrong. Our proxy reads the gross-margin trend as flat (a four-period series of 59.2%, 57.4%, 58.5%, 58.6% and a three-year change of minus 0.6 percentage points) because it averages fiscal years that include the depressed 2025 quarters; Teradyne's actual reported gross margin in the June-2026 quarter was 59.79% ($794.6M of gross profit on $1,329.0M of revenue), up 256 basis points from 57.23% a year earlier, exactly matching the company's stated 'up 250 basis points year-over-year', with the September quarter guided to 58-59% and the full year to roughly 59%. Two further proxy errors matter: the screener's price-to-free-cash-flow of 128 times and fair value of $88 are built on stale fiscal-year cash flow, whereas on trailing twelve-month free cash flow of $800M the real multiple is about 80 times; and the screener's net-debt figure is superseded by roughly $255M of net cash. One company figure runs the other way: management cited capital expenditure of '$26 million' for the June quarter while the filed cash-flow statement shows $90.7M of property and equipment purchases ($155.4M for the half). Half-year free cash flow ties exactly to the company's $579M, so this is a narrower internal definition rather than a misstatement, but it flatters how capital-light the quarter appears.
gm_trajectory: Expanding margin on doubling revenue — the signature of pricing power, not commoditisation. Gross margin went from 57.23% in the June-2025 quarter to 59.79% in June 2026 (plus 256 basis points) while revenue over the same span went from $652M to $1,329M (plus 104%). The honest caveats, both volunteered by the chief financial officer rather than dragged out of her: the March-2026 quarter's 60.9% contained non-recurring, non-operational benefits that will not repeat; the September quarter is guided down to 58-59% on product mix and new-product launches; and 'memory is going to continue to be a strain from an overall margin perspective… we expect that will continue in 2027.'
bull_thesis:
Teradyne is the second of two credible suppliers of the machines that test advanced semiconductors, and it has just finished converting itself from a mobile-phone cycle proxy into an artificial-intelligence infrastructure proxy. The evidence is unusually hard. June-2026 quarter revenue of $1.329 billion was up 104% year over year with earnings per share of $2.47 up over 300%; chip-test revenue alone was $1.122 billion, of which compute is now 70% of the chip-test product line and grew nearly 600% from a year earlier. Both 2026 quarters came in above the top of guidance, extending a run of seven earnings beats in seven quarters, and the June quarter beat the consensus estimate of $2.04 by 21% on revenue 9.3% above expectations.

The structural argument has three legs. First, test is taking a rising share of chip-industry capital spending — roughly 4% in 2023, 7% in 2025 and 8% in the first five months of 2026 — because advanced packaging stacks more chips into a single package, and one latent defect ruins an entire accelerator. More test insertions per device is a durable mix shift, not a cycle. Second, the customers themselves are handing Teradyne share: the largest compute buyers now want two qualified test suppliers for supply-chain resilience. That produced the first merchant graphics-processor production order in the March-2026 quarter, shipped and installed in June, and a completed correlation (the final technical validation step) at a second large hyperscaler. Management's four-stage qualification path runs nine to twelve months to a production ramp, which puts both of these into 2027 revenue. Third, memory: the June quarter set a third consecutive record above $200 million at $212 million, the 2026 memory test market is expected to be more than 40% larger than 2025, and the chief financial officer disclosed a book-to-bill ratio in memory 'over two' — two dollars of orders for every dollar shipped. That is the single hardest order-book datapoint in the file and it points up.

The forensic quality is what separates this from the usual promoted story in this sector. Diluted share count fell from 163.5 million to 157.7 million over two years — there is no dilution here at all. Repurchases were $243.8 million and $183.4 million in the two quarters when the stock traded roughly $90-200, then $5.5 million and $68.7 million when it traded $250-400: management bought heavily at the low and stepped back at the high, which almost nobody does. A $200 million short-term borrowing taken in September 2025 was repaid by March 2026; the company now carries roughly $255 million of net cash and $517 million of cash and investments. Capital spending is 5.9% of revenue — there is no half-built plant and no sustaining-capital hole. Returns on invested capital have gone from 22% to 31%.

What must hold for the bull case: artificial-intelligence data-centre capital spending must keep compounding (Alphabet's raise of its 2026 capital plan to as much as $205 billion, which lifted the whole test complex on 2026-08-04, is the current evidence); the compute order pause management has flagged must genuinely be timing and the surge must arrive in the first half of 2027; the second-hyperscaler and merchant-graphics wins must convert from correlation into volume; and the test share of chip-industry capital spending must settle at the upper rather than lower end of the 7-9% band management named. If those hold, 2027 revenue of roughly $6.9 billion at a 33% operating margin supports earnings near $12.45 a share, and a multiple in line with Advantest's roughly 40 times forward earnings puts the shares near $500.
bear_thesis:
The business is excellent and the price is the problem. At $404.86 the shares are up roughly 366% over twelve months and 121% this year, and carry a $63.9 billion market value against trailing free cash flow of $800 million — 79 times — and 43 times trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Nothing in the operating record is broken; what is stretched is the expectation embedded in the multiple.

The near-term arithmetic is the first problem, and it is management's own. September-quarter guidance is $1.2-1.3 billion of revenue against $1.329 billion just delivered, earnings per share of $1.85-2.15 against $2.47, gross margin of 58-59% against 59.8%, and an operating margin of 28-30% against 33.7%. Applying the company's own 'first half is 50-52% of the year' framing to first-half revenue of $2.611 billion implies full-year revenue near $5.1 billion, which leaves the December quarter at roughly $1.26 billion — flat with September. So the second half of 2026 is guided down on every line, and the cause is named: 'order timing in compute,' with 'the next surge for these customers expected to be in the first half of 2027.' That is a two-to-three quarter earnings air pocket, and management is deliberately holding operating expenses up through it (29-30% of sales in the September quarter, with December 'comparable') to staff for 2027. Falling revenue meeting a fixed cost base is negative operating leverage by choice.

The second problem is that the chief executive has already warned against the market's central extrapolation. Test's share of chip-industry capital spending ran 4% to 7% to 8% in three years; asked directly, Smith said it will 'settle somewhere in the 7% to 9% range, but it is not going to continue to go up from there,' and for 2027 specifically 'it is possible that next year that could revert down to 6, 7% or so.' A reversion from 8% to 6.5% is a roughly 19% haircut to the addressable market — before any change in the underlying capital-spending number. Compounding that, blended share is not rising: 'in terms of SoC, it is probably going to be pretty flat, maybe a slight incremental gain for us year-on-year,' because 'the part of the market that is growing most strongly is the part of the market where we are starting with the lowest share.' The market is paying a share-gain multiple for a share-flat business.

The third problem is structural fragility in the order book. Tester lead times are roughly sixteen weeks. Smith's own explanation for why he cannot forecast — customers 'are holding back on the orders for the test equipment' until wafers are actually flowing — means Teradyne has almost no contracted backlog to fall back on. Outside the memory book-to-bill, no consolidated backlog figure is disclosed anywhere in six calls. Add three customers at roughly 10% of revenue each, an acknowledged concentration into 'a smaller number of very large… device programs,' and 90.7 days of receivables with a $322 million receivables build in a single quarter, and a demand stumble arrives as a cash problem before it arrives as an order problem. The September-2025 quarter, when free cash flow was $2.4 million on $769 million of revenue purely on working capital, is the template.

Pricing the downside with numbers. Commodities here are input costs, not revenue: Teradyne buys copper, gold-plated contactors and memory and logic components for its testers. Roughly 300 basis points of cost inflation on an estimated $2.1 billion of 2027 cost of revenue is about $63 million, or 4% of operating income — real but second-order, and the current memory price spike does double damage because management already cites 'memory pricing and availability affecting end market demand' in mobile, the segment guided to decline. The dominant adverse path is order deferral, not input cost. In a 2027 digestion year, chip-test revenue falls from a base case near $5.10 billion to $3.70 billion. At roughly 60% incremental gross margin that is $840 million of gross profit removed, against an operating expense base management has committed to holding near $1.48 billion. Operating income falls from about $1.9 billion to roughly $0.85 billion and earnings per share from about $10.35 to about $5.35. Attach the multiples such a year commands — chip-test at 6.5 times sales, product test at 4 times, robotics at 3 times — and the parts total roughly $175 a share, a 57% decline. That is not a fantasy scenario: this stock's own 52-week low is $103.33, it fell about 30% in the month into 2026-07-20, and in the 2022 cycle it fell 57% peak to trough.

Finally, the segment this name is nominally classified under is its weakest. Robotics is $100 million a quarter, growing 33% against a company growing 104%, and has been promised at breakeven three years running — $440 million of revenue in 2024, $365 million in 2025, 'aiming at breakeven' in 2026 — on a roughly $400 million run-rate. What confirms the bear case: a September or December quarter that misses the guided range, any deferral language on the first-half-2027 compute surge, a Q4-call target earnings model that anchors below the market's implied 2027, or a receivables build that outpaces revenue growth a second consecutive quarter.

Semiconductor Test at $5.75 billion of 2027 revenue (the June-quarter run-rate of $4.49 billion growing about 28% as the compute surge lands in the first half of 2027 and memory capacity additions convert the above-two book-to-bill) at 12.0 times enterprise value to sales, a meaningful discount to Advantest's roughly 18 times, gives $69.0 billion or $438 a share. sop_bear: $175 a share, assuming the chain regime turns — chip-industry capital spending digests, test's share of it reverts from 8% toward 6.5% as the chief executive himself said it might, the compute order pause extends rather than resolves, and memory capacity additions pause once the current wave of fabs is equipped. Semiconductor Test at $3.70 billion of 2027 revenue (down 18% from the current run-rate; the company's 2023 analogue was a 30% decline) at 6.5 times enterprise value to sales — roughly where the group traded in the 2023-24 trough — gives $24.05 billion or $153 a share. Product Test at $0.45 billion at 4.0 times gives $1.80 billion or $11. Robotics at $0.40 billion at 3.0 times gives $1.20 billion or $8, reflecting a segment that returns to losses below its own stated breakeven bar. Net cash adds $2. Total $27.3 billion, or about $174. The balance sheet is not the risk in this scenario: with net cash, no debt maturities and capital spending at 5.9% of revenue, a downturn costs earnings and multiple, not solvency.
sop_fair_value: $355 a share (roughly a $56 billion enterprise value), about 12% below the current $404.86.
sop_breakdown: Base case, valuing 2027 by its parts against 157.7 million diluted shares. Semiconductor Test — the SoC, memory and integrated-systems businesses, $1.122 billion of revenue in the June quarter — at $5.10 billion of 2027 revenue, up about 14% from the current run-rate: the first-half-2027 compute surge and the memory capacity build are credited, but so is management's own warning that test's share of chip-industry capital spending settles at 7-9% and that blended share is flat rather than rising. risk_reward: Unfavourable at today's price. From $404.86 the adverse case at $175 is $229.86 of downside; the base-case fair value at $355 sits $49.86 BELOW the current price, so there is no upside to fair value at all — the shares already trade about 14% through our base case. Even against the favourable case at $500 the gain is $95.14 versus $229.86 of risk. The picture only turns attractive on a pullback: at $330 the risk is $155 and the base-case gain is $25 with $170 to the bull case; at $300 the risk is $125 against $55 to base and $200 to bull, which is where this becomes a position worth owning.
catalyst_status_note: The load-bearing events have already happened and the re-rating has been paid. What remains ahead is scheduled but not binding: the third-quarter report in late October 2026, and the fourth-quarter call in early 2027 at which management said it will publish an updated target earnings model. Per this lane's rules the status is descriptive only and carries no weight in the verdict; the dated-event book is handled elsewhere.
peer_comps_note: The assigned chain map lists ABB, FANUC, Yaskawa, Zebra, Cohu, Advantest and ATS as true competitors, but only two of those are economically comparable to where Teradyne actually earns its money. Chip test is 84% of revenue, so Advantest is the reference asset: it trades at roughly 39.6 times forward earnings and about 62 times trailing (per July-2026 market data), on a ¥22.4 trillion (roughly $150 billion) market value, and it fell 1.4% on the Tokyo session of 2026-08-04 after a more-than-16% rally. Teradyne at $404.86 sits at roughly 45 times our 2026 estimate and 39 times a base 2027 — a discount to Advantest that is deserved, because Advantest holds the stronger position in the fastest-growing compute sockets and Teradyne's chief executive concedes blended share is flat. Cohu, the small chip-test and handler comparable, is a $2.5 billion company trading 30% below its 52-week high and is not a valuation anchor for a $63.9 billion franchise. Onto Innovation at $14.4 billion and KLA at $254 billion frame the broader test-and-inspection band; both rallied 6-7% on 2026-08-04 in the same sector move, confirming the day's gain was beta, not news. On the automation side the peer set argues for restraint rather than enthusiasm: FANUC's market value has fallen to roughly ¥5.77 trillion and its shares trade 30% below their 52-week high, ABB is near its highs at $184 billion, and Zebra — the closest listed comparable to the MiR autonomous-mobile-robot business — is a $17.2 billion company that had a 24% single-day move. Applying that band, our base multiples of 10.0 times sales for chip test, 5.5 for product test and 4.0 for robotics are consistent with where the true competitors actually clear, and the implied 34 times base-2027 earnings for the whole company is a full multiple by any of these references.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is on the multiple, not the direction — an uncomfortable place to sit, because it means conceding almost everything the bulls say about the business.

The street's central assumption is that test's rising share of chip-industry capital spending continues. Consensus targets have marched from an average of $304.77 over the past year to $468.50 over the past quarter, with Susquehanna taking the street high to $550 from $415 in the past week explicitly on a raised chip-equipment spending forecast, and Goldman Sachs at $465 on 2026-07-28. That is a straight extrapolation of the 4%-to-7%-to-8% ramp. Teradyne's own chief executive told analysts on 2026-07-29 that it will 'settle somewhere in the 7% to 9% range, but it is not going to continue to go up from there,' and that for 2027 'it is possible that next year that could revert down to 6, 7% or so.' Nobody on the call followed up. A move from 8% back to 6.5% takes roughly 19% out of the addressable market before any change in the underlying capital-spending number, and it lands precisely in the year the price is discounting.

The second wrong assumption is that share gains are arriving now. The design-win headlines — the first merchant graphics-processor order, correlation completed at a second hyperscaler — are real and are being priced as if they convert immediately. Asked directly by UBS what share to model, Smith said chip-test share is 'probably going to be pretty flat, maybe a slight incremental gain for us year-on-year,' that the effect shows up 'in 2027… but it is going to be gradual… socket by socket,' and gave the reason: 'the part of the market that is growing most strongly is the part of the market where we are starting with the lowest share.' Even winning every fight, blended share can go sideways. And the mechanism producing the wins is not proprietary — Smith on why the door opened at all: 'customers' desire to have more resilience in their supply chain. That's why we were invited to the dance.' Dual-sourcing is symmetric; it lets rivals into Teradyne's accounts on the same logic.

The third is that the second half of 2026 is noise. Guidance says otherwise on every line — revenue $1.2-1.3 billion against $1.329 billion delivered, earnings per share $1.85-2.15 against $2.47, gross margin 58-59% against 59.8%, operating margin 28-30% against 33.7% — with operating expenses deliberately held up through it. Two of the past five price targets, Morgan Stanley's $397 on 2026-07-30 and two $420s the same day, are already below where the stock now trades; the freshest work is not chasing.

Where we disagree in Teradyne's favour, and it deserves stating: the memory story is better and more durable than the compute story the street obsesses over. The book-to-bill ratio in memory was above two in the June quarter, the 2026 memory test market is set to be more than 40% larger than 2025, memory customers are 'planning capacity additions further out in time,' and NAND flash is inflecting after years of dormancy — all of which is longer-dated and less lumpy than the compute programmes that swing quarters. And the per-share arithmetic compounds quietly: the share count is down 3.5% in two years, with the buying concentrated at the lows. The business is better than its reputation was a year ago. The stock is no longer cheap enough for that to matter.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are guided to be worse than the last three, and there is no financial distress in the picture at all — this is an earnings and multiple valley, not a solvency one.

The September-2026 quarter, reporting late October, is the first sequential step down of the cycle: revenue guided to $1.2-1.3 billion against $1.329 billion delivered, earnings per share $1.85-2.15 against $2.47, gross margin 58-59% against 59.8%, operating margin 28-30% against 33.7%. Applying management's own 'first half is 50-52% of the year' framing to first-half revenue of $2.611 billion implies a full year near $5.1 billion and therefore a December quarter of roughly $1.26 billion — flat with September. So the market is being asked to absorb two consecutive quarters of no sequential growth and a roughly 20% lower earnings run-rate than the print that caused the re-rating, in a stock that has risen 366% in twelve months.

The cost side makes it worse by design. Operating expenses are guided to 29-30% of sales in September and 'comparable' in December, up from 26.8% in the June quarter, because management is staffing for 2027 growth. That is a defensible investment decision and it is unambiguously negative operating leverage in the interim. Gross margin is guided down on product mix as the lower-margin segments — auto and industrial, integrated systems test, product test, robotics and memory — grow into the second half while high-margin compute pauses. The chief financial officer has said plainly that memory 'is going to continue to be a strain from an overall margin perspective… we expect that will continue in 2027.'

There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall. The company holds roughly $255 million of net cash and $517 million of cash and investments, repaid its only borrowing ($200 million, taken September 2025) by March 2026, generated $579 million of free cash flow in the first half, and spends 5.9% of revenue on capital equipment. The dividend costs $20 million a quarter. Nothing here breaks.

The genuine cash risk is working capital. Receivables run at 90.7 days and the March-2026 quarter absorbed a $322 million receivables build on $1,282 million of revenue. The September-2025 quarter is the cautionary template: free cash flow of $2.4 million on $769 million of revenue, entirely on working capital. With three customers at roughly 10% of revenue each and business concentrating further into a few very large device programmes, a single programme slipping shows up as uncollected receivables one to two quarters before it shows up as absent orders. Watch the receivables line more closely than the order commentary.

The macro overlay is the ordinary one for this chain: commodities are input costs here, not revenue. Rising copper, gold-plated contactor and memory-component prices raise the cost of building a tester — roughly 300 basis points on an estimated $2.1 billion of 2027 cost of revenue is about $63 million, or 4% of operating income. The memory price spike does double damage, because management already cites 'memory pricing and availability affecting end market demand' in mobile, the one segment guided to decline outright. Second-order against volume, but it runs the wrong way at the wrong time.
positioning_washout:
The shareholder base has been completely replaced over twelve months, and the replacement base is the fast-moving kind.

This was a $16 billion cyclical value name trading near $103 a year ago. It is now a $63.9 billion artificial-intelligence infrastructure vehicle, up 366% over 52 weeks and 121% this year, that moved 10.7% on 2026-08-04 on somebody else's capital-spending announcement. Nothing about that ownership is sticky. There is no yield-focused base to force out — the dividend costs $20 million a quarter against a $63.9 billion market value, roughly 0.13%, so the classic dividend-cut liquidation mechanic does not exist here. There is no leverage, no covenant, no index-deletion risk. The washout mechanism is momentum unwind, plain and simple.

The unwind is not hypothetical; it has already run twice this year. The stock fell about 30% in the month into 2026-07-20, alongside the rest of the artificial-intelligence chip supply chain, and then gapped from a $320.65 close to a $367.90 open on 2026-07-29 after the earnings beat. A stock that routinely travels 30% in either direction inside a month, at 45 times current-year earnings, does not need bad news to hand a patient buyer a better price — it only needs a quarter without an upside surprise, which is exactly what the September guidance describes.

The filings show the systematic money already trimming into the strength rather than chasing it. In the most recent reported quarter Arrowstreet Capital cut its position 41.6%, Bank of Nova Scotia cut 76.7%, Amova Asset Management cut 49.5% and Dai-ichi Life cut 19.3%. These are quantitative and rebalancing flows rather than fundamental exits, and they are the natural sellers when a position triples inside a portfolio.

Insiders are on the same side. Open-market activity is zero purchases against 32 sales totalling 36,970 shares. On a stock up four-fold that is unremarkable behaviour, but it is worth registering that the people with the best information are not adding here. The one genuinely contrary signal is corporate: the company itself spent $427 million on repurchases across the two quarters when the stock traded roughly $90-200 and only $74 million across the two quarters at $250-400. Management's own buying pattern says the same thing our valuation does.
forcing_function:
Two dated events, both of which cut against the current price before they can support it.

The first is the third-quarter 2026 report, due in late October 2026 (management's quiet period begins 2026-09-11, which brackets the date). This is the quarter guided to fall sequentially on revenue, earnings, gross margin and operating margin — the first negative print of the new cycle. The question it answers is narrow and important: is the compute pause genuinely 'order timing' with the surge intact for the first half of 2027, or is it the beginning of a digestion phase? Any softening of the first-half-2027 language is the trigger that resets the multiple.

The second, and the larger one, is the fourth-quarter 2026 call in late January or early February 2027, at which management has twice committed to publishing an updated target earnings model. Smith, 2026-07-29: 'this sets the approach for how we will be updating our target earnings model which we will share in our Q4 earnings call,' and Turner: 'we remain confident in achieving our target earnings model at an accelerated pace.' The existing framework is built around a $12-14 billion addressable market and roughly $6 billion of company revenue. The new one will put a number on the $20 billion market Smith sketched for the end of the decade, and on what share of it Teradyne expects. That single disclosure is what re-anchors the multiple in either direction, and it is the reason to be watching rather than owning right now — buying ahead of a number management has deliberately declined to give is paying for information you do not have.

A third, softer trigger sits between them: the first-half-2027 compute surge itself. If the merchant graphics-processor ramp and the second-hyperscaler qualification convert to volume on the nine-to-twelve-month schedule management described, the March-2027 quarter is where it becomes visible in revenue rather than in slides.
moderator_conclusion:
This is one of the cleanest operating stories to come through this lane, and it is a wait, not a buy — the disagreement is entirely about price.

Start with what is genuinely true. Teradyne has converted itself from a mobile-phone cycle proxy into an artificial-intelligence infrastructure supplier in about eight quarters, and the conversion is verified in the filings, not just the slides: June-quarter revenue of $1.329 billion, up 104% year over year, with earnings per share of $2.47 up over 300%, both above the top of guidance, extending seven beats in seven quarters. The lie detector for this lane is the gross-margin direction, and it points the right way — 57.23% to 59.79% year over year, up 256 basis points, while revenue doubled. Expanding margin on doubling volume is pricing power in a supply-constrained niche; commoditisation looks like the opposite. Our own deterministic proxy reads this trend as flat and is simply wrong, because it averages fiscal years that include the depressed 2025 quarters.

The capital discipline is better still, and it is the rarest thing in the file. Diluted shares fell from 163.5 million to 157.7 million over two years — no dilution of any kind, which clears the primary failure mode in this sector. Management repurchased $243.8 million and $183.4 million of stock in the two quarters when the shares traded roughly $90-200, and only $5.5 million and $68.7 million when they traded $250-400. Buying heavily at the low and stepping back at the high is behaviour almost no management team exhibits; most do the reverse. The company carries net cash, repaid its only borrowing, spends 5.9% of revenue on capital equipment, and has no sustaining-capital hole to fund. On the order book, the one hard number disclosed is strong — memory book-to-bill above two in the June quarter, in a market management expects to be more than 40% larger this year than last — though it sits alongside an important structural weakness: tester lead times are roughly sixteen weeks, so there is almost no contracted backlog by construction, and outside memory none is disclosed.

Now the price. At $404.86 the market value is $63.9 billion — 79 times trailing free cash flow, 43 times trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, about 45 times our 2026 estimate and 39 times a base 2027. Valued by its parts on 2027 — chip test at $5.10 billion of revenue and 10 times sales, product test at $0.55 billion and 5.5 times, robotics at $0.50 billion and 4 times, plus $255 million of net cash — the business is worth about $355 a share. The stock trades roughly 14% through that. The adverse case, in which chip-industry capital spending digests and test's share of it reverts from 8% toward 6.5%, puts chip-test revenue at $3.70 billion, earnings near $5.35 a share and the parts at about $175 — a 57% decline, which sounds violent until you note this stock's own 52-week low is $103.33, that it fell about 30% in the single month into 2026-07-20, and that it fell 57% peak to trough in the 2022 cycle.

The decisive evidence is that the chief executive has already warned against the market's central assumption. Test's share of chip-industry capital spending ran 4% to 7% to 8% in three years; Smith said on 2026-07-29 that it 'is not going to continue to go up from there' and could 'revert down to 6, 7% or so' in 2027. He also said blended chip-test share is 'probably going to be pretty flat, maybe a slight incremental gain,' because the fastest-growing part of the market is where Teradyne starts with the lowest share. Meanwhile the street has marched its average target from $304.77 over the past year to $468.50 over the past quarter, with a new street high of $550 set this week on a raised equipment-spending forecast. Two of the five freshest targets — Morgan Stanley's $397 and two $420s, all dated 2026-07-30 — already sit at or below where the stock now trades. The 10.7% gain on 2026-08-04 was a sector move on Alphabet's capital-spending raise, which lifted Advantest more than 16% and KLA and Onto Innovation 6-7%; it was beta, not news about Teradyne.

The timing call, therefore, is to wait, and the level is specific because the stock supplies it regularly: accumulate below $330, roughly 18% under today's price and a modest discount to our $355 base case, which this name traded through as recently as late July. Below $300 it becomes genuinely attractive — $125 of risk to the adverse case against $55 to base and $200 to the favourable case. The two dated events to watch are the third-quarter report in late October 2026, the first guided sequential decline of the cycle, and the fourth-quarter call in early 2027, where management will finally publish the updated target earnings model. Buying ahead of a number management has deliberately declined to give is paying for information you do not have.

One last note on the classification. This name is filed under factory automation, and that is its weakest business by a wide margin — robotics is $100 million a quarter growing 33% against a company growing 104%, and has been promised at breakeven three years running without delivering. Almost all of the value, and all of the argument, is in chip test. Judge it as a test-equipment franchise at a cyclical high, not as a robotics story. Excellent company, wrong entry price. Wait for the wash-out; this one reliably provides it.
